Question  
Draw a circle of radius 2.7 cm. Draw a tangent to the circle at any point on it.

Method  
We use the fact: a tangent to a circle at point M is perpendicular to the radius OM (O = centre, M = point on the circle). To get the perpendicular at M with ruler and compass, mark two points A and B on the line OM equidistant from M by drawing an arc with centre M, then construct the perpendicular bisector of AB — that bisector passes through M and is perpendicular to OM. This bisector is the required tangent.

Working (construction steps)

1. Draw the circle:
   - With a compass set to 2.7 cm, draw a circle with centre O. Mark any point M on the circumference.

2. Mark two points on line OM:
   - Place the compass at M and choose any convenient radius (for example 1.2 cm). With this radius draw an arc that meets the straight line OM at two points; label them A and B. (Since the arc is centered at M, AM = BM.)

3. Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB:
   - With the compass centered at A, and radius greater than half AB, draw an arc above and below line AB.
   - With the same radius and center B, draw two arcs that meet the previous arcs; label their intersection points C and D.
   - Join C and D with a straight line. CD is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

4. Identify the tangent:
   - CD passes through M (because M is the midpoint of AB) and is perpendicular to AB (and so to OM). Therefore CD is perpendicular to OM at M.
   - The line CD is the tangent to the circle at M. Extend CD as needed.

Reason (why this works)  
- AM = BM by construction, so M is the midpoint of AB. The line joining the intersection points C and D of equal-radius arcs from A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB; hence it passes through M and is perpendicular to AB. Because AB lies on OM, CD is perpendicular to OM at M. Since a tangent at a point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point, CD is the tangent at M.

Final answer  
A circle of radius 2.7 cm with centre O and a tangent at point M on the circle: the line through M perpendicular to OM (constructed as above) is the required tangent. 

Diagram cue: A textbook diagram may show the circle, O, M, points A, B, and the perpendicular bisector CD. The construction above explains how to obtain those points and the tangent; no additional numerical values from the diagram were assumed.

Question  
Draw a circle of radius 3.6 cm. Draw a tangent to the circle at any point on it without using the centre.

Given  
A circle of radius 3.6 cm (you may draw it by choosing a centre O and opening the compass to 3.6 cm).

To construct  
A tangent to the circle at a chosen point K on the circle, without using the centre in the construction of the tangent.

Construction / Steps
1. Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.6 cm. Mark any point K on the circumference; this is the point at which the tangent is required.  
2. Choose any other point A on the circle (A ≠ K).  
3. Choose a third point B on the circle different from A and K (B ≠ A, K).  
4. Join A to B and A to K and B to K by straight lines (draw the chords AK and BK, and the chord AB if helpful). We need the inscribed angle subtended by chord AK at point B, that is ∠KBA.  
5. Copy the angle ∠KBA at the point K with one ray of the copied angle along KA:
   - With vertex B, draw a small arc that cuts BA and BK at two points, say P and Q.  
   - With the same radius, draw a similar arc centered at K, cutting ray KA at point R.  
   - With the compass, measure the distance between P and Q. With that distance and centres at R and the appropriate second point, mark the intersection that gives the direction of the other side of the copied angle. (This is the standard procedure for copying an angle using compass and straightedge.)  
   - Draw the ray from K through this intersection; let this ray be l. Make sure you copy the angle on the side of KA away from the interior of the circle (so l lies outside touching the circle at K).  
6. The ray l constructed in step 5 is the required tangent at K.

Proof / Reasoning
By the alternate segment theorem (tangent–chord theorem): the angle between a tangent at a point K and the chord through K equals the angle in the opposite arc subtended by that chord. Here, the angle between the tangent at K and chord KA equals the inscribed angle ∠KBA. We copied ∠KBA at K with one side along KA; therefore the other side of the copied angle is the tangent at K. No use of the centre O was made in this tangent construction.

Diagram cue  
The textbook figure shows a tangent l at K and chords through K and other points; the construction above reproduces that situation using only chord AK, an inscribed angle at B, and copying that angle at K.

Result  
A tangent to the circle at the chosen point K is constructed without using the centre.

Question
Draw a circle of radius 3.3 cm. Draw a chord PQ of length 6.6 cm. Draw tangents to the circle at points P and Q. Write your observation about the tangents.

Method
1. Construct the circle with centre O and radius 3.3 cm.
2. Draw a chord PQ of length 6.6 cm (note 6.6 cm = 2 × 3.3 cm).
3. Construct the tangents at P and Q by drawing lines through P and Q each perpendicular to the corresponding radius (OP and OQ).
4. Observe the relation between the two tangent lines.

Working
1. Radius = 3.3 cm, so diameter = 2 × 3.3 = 6.6 cm. Because the given chord PQ has length 6.6 cm, PQ must be a diameter of the circle. Hence O, P and Q are collinear and OP and OQ lie on the same straight line.
2. Property: A tangent at a point on a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact. So the tangent at P is a line through P perpendicular to OP; the tangent at Q is a line through Q perpendicular to OQ.
3. Since OP and OQ lie on the same line, both tangents are perpendicular to the same straight line. Two distinct lines each perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other.

(Construction detail for the perpendicular through a point on a line using compass and ruler:
- Extend the line OP slightly past P. Mark two points A and B on this line, one on each side of P, at equal distances from P.
- With center A and radius > AP draw an arc above the line; with center B and same radius draw another arc so the two arcs intersect at X (and similarly below produce Y).
- Join X and Y; the line XY passes through P and is perpendicular to OP. Repeat at Q.)

Final answer
PQ is a diameter. The tangents drawn at P and Q are perpendicular to the same line (the diameter OPQ), therefore the two tangents are parallel.

Question 5

Given
- A circle of radius 3.4 cm (centre O).
- A chord MN of length 5.7 cm to be constructed in the circle.
- Construct tangents at the points M and N.

To construct
- A circle with radius 3.4 cm, a chord MN of length 5.7 cm on it, and the tangents to the circle at M and N.

Proof / Steps (construction with justification)
1. Draw the circle:
   - Draw a point O to be the centre.
   - With compass set to 3.4 cm and centre O, draw the circle. (Call this circle Γ.)

2. Place one end of the chord:
   - Mark any point M on the circumference of Γ. (Any point on the circle is acceptable.)

3. Locate the other end N so that MN = 5.7 cm:
   - With the compass set to 5.7 cm and centre at M, draw an arc that meets the circle Γ at a point N (choose the intersection different from M). This intersection N satisfies MN = 5.7 cm by construction, so MN is the required chord.
   - (Remark: Because 5.7 cm < 2 × 3.4 cm = 6.8 cm is not required; the existence of intersection follows from the circle-centre distance being 3.4 cm and 5.7 cm satisfying the circle–circle intersection condition. If your first choice of M gives the other intersection on the extension, choose a different M.)

4. Draw the radii to the chord endpoints:
   - Join O to M and O to N by straight lines. OM and ON are radii.

5. Construct the tangent at M:
   - A tangent at a point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point. So we must draw the line through M perpendicular to OM.
   - To construct the perpendicular through M:
     a. With centre M and any convenient radius, draw an arc that cuts the line OM at two points A and B placed on opposite sides of M.
     b. With the compass set to a radius larger than half AB, draw two arcs with centres A and B so that these arcs meet at two points P and Q on opposite sides of OM.
     c. Join P and Q by a straight line. This line passes through M and is perpendicular to OM. This is the tangent to Γ at M.
   - Label this tangent as the line tM.

6. Construct the tangent at N:
   - Repeat step 5 with centre N and radius ON:
     a. With centre N draw an arc cutting ON at two points C and D on either side of N.
     b. With centres C and D and equal radii draw arcs that meet at points R and S.
     c. Join R and S; the line through R and S is perpendicular to ON and so is the tangent at N.
   - Label this tangent as the line tN.

Justification
- By construction MN = 5.7 cm.
- The line constructed through M perpendicular to OM is tangent because a radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent at that point. Same for N.

Diagram cue
- If a diagram is provided, it will typically show circle Γ with centre O, chord MN, radii OM and ON, and the two tangent lines at M and N perpendicular to OM and ON respectively.

Result
- Circle Γ with centre O and radius 3.4 cm is drawn.
- Points M and N on Γ are chosen so that MN = 5.7 cm.
- Tangents at M and N are constructed as the lines through M and N respectively perpendicular to the radii OM and ON. These are the required tangents.

Question 6  
Draw a circle with centre P and radius 3.4 cm. Take point Q at a distance 5.5 cm from the centre. Construct tangents to the circle from point Q.

Given
- A circle with centre P and radius 3.4 cm.
- A point Q such that PQ = 5.5 cm (so Q lies outside the given circle because 5.5 > 3.4).

To construct
- The two tangents from Q to the given circle, meeting the circle at points R and S.

Construction steps (compass and ruler)
1. Draw the given circle with centre P and radius 3.4 cm.
2. With the ruler, draw the segment PQ of length 5.5 cm so that Q is placed at the required distance from P.
3. Construct the midpoint M of segment PQ:
   - With the compass set to a radius greater than half PQ, draw arcs above and below PQ with centre P.
   - With the same radius, draw arcs above and below PQ with centre Q.
   - Join the two intersection points of these arcs; this line is the perpendicular bisector of PQ. Its intersection with PQ is the midpoint M.
4. With centre M and radius MP (= MQ = 1/2 PQ), draw the circle having PQ as diameter.
5. Let the circle from step 4 intersect the given circle (centre P, radius 3.4 cm) at two points; label them R and S.
6. Join Q to R and Q to S using the ruler. QR and QS are the required tangents.

Proof / Justification
- By construction, R and S lie on the circle whose diameter is PQ. For any point X on a circle with diameter PQ, the angle ∠PXQ is a right angle (Thales' theorem). Hence ∠PRQ = 90° and ∠PSQ = 90°.
- Since PR and PS are radii of the given circle and they meet QR and QS respectively at right angles, QR and QS are perpendicular to the radii at the points of contact; that is the defining property of a tangent line. Therefore QR and QS are tangents to the given circle at R and S.
- Because Q is outside the circle (PQ > radius), there are exactly two tangents from Q to the circle, which we have constructed.

Working (numerical check)
- Tangent length QR (and QS) can be found from right triangle PRQ:
  QR = sqrt(PQ^2 − PR^2) = sqrt(5.5^2 − 3.4^2)
     = sqrt(30.25 − 11.56) = sqrt(18.69) ≈ 4.32 cm.
  This is a check; the construction produces segments QR and QS of this length.

Result
- The lines QR and QS constructed above are the two tangents from Q to the circle with centre P and radius 3.4 cm.

Question
Draw a circle with centre P and radius 4.1 cm. From a point Q such that PQ = 7.3 cm construct the two tangents from Q to the circle.

Method
Use the fact that if QR is a tangent at R, then PR ⟂ QR. Hence in triangle PQR the angle at R is 90°, so R lies on the circle having PQ as diameter (Thales' result). Thus the intersection points of the circle with centre P (radius 4.1 cm) and the circle having PQ as diameter give the tangent points. Joining those points to Q gives the required tangents.

Working (step-by-step construction and justification)
1. Draw point P and draw a circle with centre P and radius 4.1 cm. This is the given circle.

2. Mark a point Q so that PQ = 7.3 cm. Join P and Q by a straight line segment PQ.

3. Construct the circle with PQ as diameter:
   - Find the midpoint M of segment PQ (by the perpendicular bisector construction).
   - Using M as centre and radius MP = MQ, draw the circle with diameter PQ. (This circle is the locus of points X for which ∠PXQ = 90°.)

4. Locate the intersection points R and S of the circle with centre P (radius 4.1 cm) and the circle with diameter PQ. (There will be two intersection points since Q is outside the given circle.)

5. Join Q to R and Q to S using straight lines. These QR and QS are the required tangents.

Justification:
- At a point of contact of a tangent with a circle the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. So PR ⟂ QR and PS ⟂ QS.
- Therefore ∠PRQ = ∠PSQ = 90°. By the converse of Thales' theorem, R and S lie on the circle with PQ as diameter. Hence the intersections found in step 4 are exactly the contact points of the tangents from Q.
- Thus QR and QS are tangents to the given circle from Q.

Extra (tangent length)
The length of each tangent segment QR = QS can be checked by right-triangle PQR:
QR = sqrt(PQ^2 − PR^2) = sqrt(7.3^2 − 4.1^2)
    = sqrt(53.29 − 16.81) = sqrt(36.48) ≈ 6.04 cm.

Diagram cue
If a figure is shown in the book, it may label P, Q, R, S and show the two circles. No other numerical values beyond PQ = 7.3 cm and radius 4.1 cm are assumed.

Final answer
Construct the circle centre P, radius 4.1 cm; construct the circle with PQ as diameter; their intersection points R and S are the tangent points. Joining Q to R and Q to S gives the two tangents. Each tangent length QR = QS ≈ 6.04 cm.

Question 1

i) The number of tangents that can be drawn to a circle at a point on the circle is ______

Method
- Use the property that a tangent at a point on a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point.
- Through a given point on a line (here the point on the circle), there is exactly one line perpendicular to a given radius.

Working
- Let O be the centre of the circle and P a point on the circle. OP is the radius to P.
- Any tangent at P must be perpendicular to OP.
- Through point P there is a unique line perpendicular to OP; no other distinct line through P can be perpendicular to OP.

Final answer
(C) 1

---

ii) The maximum number of tangents that can be drawn to a circle from a point outside it is ______

Method
- Consider an external point and the lines from it that just touch the circle (tangents). Use symmetry or the fact that the tangency condition yields up to two distinct contact points.

Working
- Let O be the centre and X an external point. Draw lines from X that meet the circle at a single point each (tangents).
- Geometrically one can construct two such tangents: one touching the circle at a point on one side, and another touching on the opposite side. Algebraically, the condition for tangency (distance and right triangle formed with radius) gives two solutions for the tangency points when X is outside.
- If X is on the circle there is exactly one tangent; if X is inside there are no tangents. From an external point the maximum is two.

Final answer
(A) 2

---

iii) If ∆ABC ~ ∆PQR and AB : PQ = 7 : 5, then ______

Method
- For similar triangles corresponding sides are proportional by the same ratio (scale factor). Compare the ratio 7:5 (>1) to decide which triangle is larger.

Working
- Given AB : PQ = 7 : 5, the scale factor from ∆PQR to ∆ABC is 7/5.
- Since 7/5 > 1, every side of ∆ABC is 7/5 times the corresponding side of ∆PQR; thus ∆ABC is larger.

Final answer
(A) ∆ABC is bigger.

Question  
Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.5 cm. Take point P at a distance 5.7 cm from the centre. Draw tangents to the circle from point P.

Method  
We will construct the tangents from P by using the property: if Q is a point on the given circle such that ∠OQP = 90°, then PQ is tangent at Q. Points Q and R where the circle with OP as diameter meets the given circle will give the required points of tangency. Construction uses compass and straightedge to find the midpoint of OP and draw the circle with OP as diameter.

Working (construction steps and reasoning)

1. Draw the given circle:
   - With centre O and radius 3.5 cm, draw circle (O).

2. Locate point P:
   - On the plane, mark point P so that OP = 5.7 cm (use ruler or set compass to 5.7 cm and mark).

3. Draw segment OP.

4. Find midpoint M of OP:
   - With compass set to a radius greater than half OP, draw two arcs centered at O and P so that the arcs meet at two points on either side of OP.
   - Join those two intersection points with a straight line. This line is the perpendicular bisector of OP and meets OP at its midpoint M.
   - Measure: MO = MP = OP/2 = 5.7/2 = 2.85 cm.

5. Draw the circle with OP as diameter:
   - With centre M and radius MO = 2.85 cm, draw a circle. This is the circle having OP as diameter.

6. Locate tangency points Q and R:
   - Let Q and R be the points where the circle (with centre M) meets the original circle (with centre O). (These two intersection points exist because OP > radius and the two circles meet in two points when OP > radius and OP < 2·radius of the constructed circle’s relation — here they intersect because of geometry of the situation.)
   - (If a supplied diagram had additional marks not given in the text, treat those as Diagram cue; we use only the given lengths and constructed midpoint.)

7. Draw the tangents:
   - Join P to Q and P to R using the ruler. Segments PQ and PR are the required tangents.

Reason why PQ and PR are tangents:
- For any point Q on the circle with OP as diameter, ∠OQP is a right angle (angle subtended by diameter OP is 90°). Hence OQ ⟂ PQ. Because OQ is a radius of the given circle and it is perpendicular to PQ at Q, PQ is tangent to the given circle at Q. Similarly PR is tangent at R.

Optional numeric check (length of tangent):
- Length of tangent PQ = √(OP^2 − OQ^2) = √(5.7^2 − 3.5^2) = √(32.49 − 12.25) = √20.24 ≈ 4.498 cm ≈ 4.50 cm.

Final answer  
Follow the construction above. The points Q and R obtained as intersections of the circle having OP as diameter with the given circle are the points of tangency; joining P to Q and P to R gives the two tangents from P to the circle.

Question
Draw any circle. Take any point A on it and construct the tangent at A without using the centre of the circle.

Method
Use the tangent–chord (alternate segment) property: the angle between a tangent at A and the chord AB equals the angle in the opposite arc subtended by chord AB. So pick two other points B and C on the circle, measure the inscribed angle ACB, and copy that angle at A with one arm along the chord AB; the copied ray will be the required tangent at A.

Working (step-by-step construction)
1. Given: a circle and a point A on it.
2. Choose two distinct points B and C on the circle, different from A.
3. Join C to A and C to B (draw segments CA and CB). This gives the inscribed angle ∠ACB.
4. We will copy ∠ACB so that its vertex is at A and one side is the chord AB. To copy the angle:
   a. With centre C and some convenient radius, draw an arc that cuts CA at D and CB at E.
   b. With the same radius, draw an arc centered at A which cuts AB at F.
   c. Measure the distance between D and E with the compass (i.e. set compass width to DE).
   d. With centre F and radius DE, draw an arc that meets the arc from step 4b at a point G.
   e. Join A to G. The ray AG makes at A an angle with AB equal to ∠ACB.
5. Choose the ray AG that goes outside the circle (the ray should not go into the interior of the circle). This ray AG is the required tangent at A.

Justification
By the tangent–chord (alternate segment) theorem, the angle between a tangent at A and the chord AB equals the angle in the opposite arc subtended by AB, which is ∠ACB. Since AG was constructed so that ∠BAG = ∠ACB, the line AG touches the circle at A and is therefore the tangent at A.

Final answer
The ray AG constructed above is the tangent to the circle at A. (Construction used only compass and straightedge; the centre of the circle was not needed.)

Diagram cue
The construction uses only points A, B, C on the circle and standard arcs for copying an angle; no additional measurements from the centre were required.

Question 4

Draw a circle of diameter 6.4 cm. Take a point R at a distance equal to its diameter from the centre. Draw tangents from point R.

Method

- Tools: ruler, compass, pencil.
- Strategy: Let O be the centre of the given circle. Draw the given circle (diameter 6.4 cm so radius 3.2 cm). Place an external point R on a ray from O at distance OR = 6.4 cm. Construct the circle with diameter OR (center M, the midpoint of OR). The intersections Q and S of this new circle with the given circle are the points of contact of the required tangents. Join RQ and RS; these are the tangents.

Working (construction steps with measurements)

1. Draw a line and mark a point O (centre of the given circle).
2. With compass set to radius 3.2 cm, draw the given circle with centre O (this is the circle of diameter 6.4 cm).
3. From O choose a ray and on it mark point R such that OR = 6.4 cm (use the ruler to measure 6.4 cm from O).
4. Find the midpoint M of segment OR (use compass or ruler: draw equal arcs from O and R and join their intersections, then draw the perpendicular bisector; where it meets OR is M). Note OM = MR = 3.2 cm.
5. With centre M and radius equal to OR/2 = 3.2 cm, draw the circle having OR as diameter.
6. Let Q and S be the two points where the circle with centre M meets the original circle with centre O.
7. Join RQ and RS using the ruler. These are the required tangent lines from R to the original circle.

Justification (why RQ and RS are tangents)

- Point Q lies on the circle having OR as diameter, so angle OQ R is an angle subtended by the diameter OR. By the theorem "angle in a semicircle is a right angle", ∠OQR = 90°. Thus OQ ⟂ QR.
- OQ is a radius of the given circle; a radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent at that point. Since OQ ⟂ QR, line RQ is tangent to the given circle at Q.
- The same reasoning applies to S, so RS is tangent at S.

Final answer

- Radius of given circle = 3.2 cm.
- Construct the circle centre O, radius 3.2 cm. Place R so that OR = 6.4 cm.
- Construct the circle with diameter OR (centre M, radius 3.2 cm). Its intersections Q and S with the original circle are tangent points.
- Lines RQ and RS are the two tangents from R to the original circle.

Question
Draw a circle with centre P. On this circle mark an arc AB of 100° (i.e. central angle ∠APB = 100°). Construct the tangents to the circle at A and at B.

Method
1. Draw a circle with centre P and choose point A on it.  
2. Construct point B on the circle so that central angle ∠APB = 100°.  
3. At A and at B construct lines perpendicular to the radii PA and PB respectively. These perpendiculars are the required tangents, because a tangent at a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

Working (step-by-step construction)
1. Draw point P. With P as centre and any convenient radius, draw circle (P).  
2. Choose a point A on the circle; mark it. Draw the radius PA.  
3. At P place a protractor, measure an angle of 100° from ray PA, and mark the direction of the second radius. Where this ray meets the circle, mark point B. (If a protractor is not to be used, construct 100° by compass-and-straightedge methods — for example combine constructions of 60° and 40° — and place the second radius accordingly.) Draw the radius PB. Now ∠APB = 100°, so arc AB measures 100°.  
4. To draw the tangent at A (compass-and-straightedge method):  
   a. With centre A and any radius greater than half the local arc, draw two arcs that cut the circle on either side of A (or simply draw two arcs centered at A that intersect the circle at two points); label the two intersection points X and Y.  
   b. With centres X and Y and the same radius (slightly larger), draw two arcs on the outside of the circle so that they meet at a point T.  
   c. Draw line AT. This line is perpendicular to PA and so is the tangent at A.  
   (Alternatively, use a set-square to draw a line through A perpendicular to PA; that line is the tangent.)  
5. Repeat the same perpendicular construction at B to obtain the tangent at B: construct two arcs from B to find points U and V, then arcs from U and V that meet at S, and draw line BS (or use a set-square to draw the perpendicular to PB through B). The resulting line is the tangent at B.

Justification
- The central angle ∠APB equals the measure of arc AB, so constructing ∠APB = 100° gives arc AB of 100°.  
- A tangent to a circle at a point is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point. Thus any line through A perpendicular to PA is a tangent at A; similarly for B.

Final answer
Lines through A and B constructed perpendicular to PA and PB respectively are the required tangents at A and B.

Question 6

Draw a circle of radius 3.4 cm and centre E. Take a point F on the circle. Take another point A such that E – F – A and FA = 4.1 cm. Draw tangents to the circle from point A.

Method

- Find the distance EA using the given EF (radius) and FA.
- Construct the circle with EA as diameter. By Thales' theorem, any point P on this diameter-circle satisfies ∠EPA = 90°, so intersections of this circle with the given circle are points of tangency.
- Join A to each intersection to obtain the two tangents.

Working (construction and reasoning)

1. Compute EA.
   - EF = radius = 3.4 cm, FA = 4.1 cm, with E–F–A collinear and F between E and A.
   - EA = EF + FA = 3.4 + 4.1 = 7.5 cm.

2. Draw the given circle.
   - With centre E and radius 3.4 cm, draw circle (call it C1).

3. Locate point A.
   - From point E draw the ray through the chosen point F and mark A on that ray so that FA = 4.1 cm (equivalently EA = 7.5 cm from E).

4. Construct the circle having EA as diameter.
   - Find the midpoint M of segment EA (half of 7.5 cm = 3.75 cm from E).
   - With centre M and radius ME = MA = 3.75 cm draw the circle (call it C2).

5. Find intersection points P and Q.
   - Circles C1 (centre E, radius 3.4 cm) and C2 (centre M, radius 3.75 cm) meet at two points; mark these intersections P and Q.
   - (Check: the two circles do intersect because |3.75 − 3.4| = 0.35 < EM = 3.75 < 3.75 + 3.4 = 7.15.)

6. Draw the tangents.
   - Join A to P and A to Q. These segments AP and AQ are the required tangents.

Reason these are tangents:
- For each intersection point (say P), points E, P, A lie on circle C2 whose diameter is EA. By Thales' theorem, ∠EPA = 90°. Thus EP is perpendicular to AP.
- EP is a radius of the original circle C1. A line through a circle’s point that is perpendicular to the radius at that point is a tangent. Therefore AP is tangent to circle C1 at P. The same argument applies to Q.

Final answer

- EA = 7.5 cm.
- Construct the circle with centre E and radius 3.4 cm. Place A so that EA = 7.5 cm along the line through F.
- Draw the circle with EA as diameter (centre at midpoint M, radius 3.75 cm). Let P and Q be its intersections with the original circle.
- Segments AP and AQ are the two tangents from A to the given circle.

Question 7

Given
- ∆ABC ~ ∆LBN.
- In ∆ABC: AB = 5.1 cm, ∠B = 40°, BC = 4.8 cm.
- AC : LN = 4 : 7 (that is, corresponding sides of the similar triangles are in ratio 4:7).

To construct
- Construct triangle ABC with the given data, and then construct triangle LBN which is similar to ∆ABC with the correspondence A ↔ L, B ↔ B, C ↔ N.

Proof / Steps (construction with reason)
1. Interpretation and plan
   - Since ∆ABC ~ ∆LBN with A ↔ L, B ↔ B, C ↔ N, vertex B is common in correspondence. Rays BA and BL are collinear (L lies on the ray BA produced) and rays BC and BN are collinear (N lies on the ray BC produced).
   - The similarity ratio (corresponding sides of ∆ABC to ∆LBN) is 4 : 7. So lengths from B scale by factor 7/4. In particular BN = (7/4) × BC and BL = (7/4) × AB. We will construct N and L by the standard proportional division (parallel-lines) method.

2. Construct ∆ABC
   a. Draw a point B.
   b. At B, construct angle ∠ABC = 40°; along one arm mark point C so that BC = 4.8 cm.
   c. Along the other arm of the 40° at B, mark point A so that AB = 5.1 cm.
   d. Join A and C to complete ∆ABC.

3. Locate N on ray BC produced such that BN = (7/4)·BC
   (Using the method of dividing a ray into equal parts and using parallel lines.)
   a. From B draw any convenient ray BX making an acute angle with BC (inside the plane).
   b. On BX, using the compass, mark seven consecutive equal segments: B1, B2, …, B7, so that BB1 = B1B2 = … = B6B7.
   c. Join B4 to C (point corresponding to 4 parts because the numerator for BC is 4).
   d. Through B7 draw a line parallel to B4C. Let this parallel meet the line through B and C (the ray BC produced beyond C) at N.
   Reason: Triangles BB4C and BB7N are similar, hence BC / BN = BB4 / BB7 = 4/7, so BN = (7/4)·BC.

4. Locate L on ray BA produced such that BL = (7/4)·AB
   a. Through N draw a line parallel to AC.
   b. Let this line meet the ray BA produced (extend BA beyond A if necessary) at L.
   Reason: Since line through N is parallel to AC, ∠LBN = ∠ABC and ∠LNB = ∠ACB, so ∆LBN ~ ∆ABC with the same correspondence; this places L on BA produced and gives BL/AB = BN/BC = 7/4.

Working (numerical checks)
- BN = (7/4) × BC = (7/4) × 4.8 = 7 × 1.2 = 8.4 cm.
- BL = (7/4) × AB = (7/4) × 5.1 = 7 × 1.275 = 8.925 cm (≈ 8.93 cm).
- (Optional) AC by cosine rule: AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 − 2·AB·BC·cos 40°
  => AC ≈ 3.397 cm, and then LN = (7/4)·AC ≈ 5.945 cm, which is consistent with the similarity.

Diagram cue
- If a textbook diagram is present, it likely shows B, C, N collinear (with N beyond C) and B, A, L collinear (with L beyond A). We have deduced these positions from the correspondence of vertices in the given similarity.

Result
- Triangle ABC constructed with AB = 5.1 cm, BC = 4.8 cm, ∠B = 40°.
- Triangle LBN constructed on the same rays with BN = 8.4 cm and BL ≈ 8.925 cm, so that ∆LBN is similar to ∆ABC in the ratio 7 : 4.

Question 8

Construct triangle PYQ with PY = 6.3 cm, YQ = 7.2 cm, PQ = 5.8 cm. Then construct triangle XYZ similar to PYQ given that YZ : YQ = 6 : 5.

Given
- PY = 6.3 cm, YQ = 7.2 cm, PQ = 5.8 cm.
- YZ : YQ = 6 : 5 (scale factor k = 6/5 = 1.2).

To construct
- ΔPYQ with the three given sides.
- ΔXYZ such that ΔXYZ ~ ΔPYQ and YZ = (6/5)·YQ.

Construction steps
1. Construct ΔPYQ.
   a. Draw a line and mark points Y and Q so that YQ = 7.2 cm.
   b. With centre Y and radius 6.3 cm draw an arc.
   c. With centre Q and radius 5.8 cm draw another arc. Let P be one intersection of these two arcs.
   d. Join P to Y and P to Q. Now ΔPYQ is constructed.

2. On a ray from Y make equal divisions to get the required ratio.
   a. From Y draw an auxiliary ray making an acute angle with YQ.
   b. Using the compass, mark six equal segments on this ray: Y1, Y2, Y3, Y4, Y5, Y6 so that YY1 = Y1Y2 = … = Y5Y6.
   (We mark six points because the numerator of the ratio is 6 while the denominator is 5.)

3. Locate point Z on YQ produced so that YZ : YQ = 6 : 5.
   a. Join Y5 to Q.
   b. Through Y6 draw a line parallel to Y5Q (use a set-square or construct a parallel with compass).
   c. This parallel meets the line YQ (produced beyond Q) at Z. Then YZ = (6/5)·YQ.

4. Locate point X so that ΔXYZ is similar to ΔPYQ.
   a. Through Z draw a line parallel to PQ.
   b. Let this line meet the ray through Y toward P (produced beyond P if necessary) at X.
   c. Join X to Z and X to Y. Then ΔXYZ is obtained.

Explanation / Reason (why this works)
- By drawing the auxiliary ray and marking six equal parts, then joining the 5th point to Q and drawing a line through the 6th point parallel to that join, we obtain YZ/YQ = 6/5 by basic properties of similar triangles (triangles formed by parallels are proportional).
- Drawing ZX parallel to PQ makes XZ ∥ PQ and XY ∥ PY (because both share Y and are rays from Y), so corresponding angles of ΔXYZ and ΔPYQ are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio YX/YP = YZ/YQ = 6/5. Therefore the two triangles are similar.

Working (numerical verification)
- Scale factor k = 6/5 = 1.2.
- YZ = k·YQ = 1.2 × 7.2 cm = 8.64 cm.
- YX = k·YP = 1.2 × 6.3 cm = 7.56 cm.
- XZ = k·PQ = 1.2 × 5.8 cm = 6.96 cm.

Result
- ΔPYQ constructed with the given sides.
- ΔXYZ constructed similar to ΔPYQ with YZ : YQ = 6 : 5.
- Corresponding side lengths of ΔXYZ are YX = 7.56 cm, YZ = 8.64 cm, XZ = 6.96 cm (these are the scaled values; construct them using the parallel/auxiliary-ray method described).

Question 1  
Find the distance between each of the following pairs of points.

i. A(2, 3), B(4, 1)  
ii. P(−5, 7), Q(−1, 3)  
iii. R(0, −3), S(0, 5/2)  
iv. L(5, −8), M(−7, −3)  
v. T(−3, 6), R(9, −10)  
vi. W(−7/2, 4), X(11, 4)

Method  
For any two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), the distance d between them is
d = √[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2].

Working

i. A(2, 3), B(4, 1)  
x2 − x1 = 4 − 2 = 2,  y2 − y1 = 1 − 3 = −2  
d = √[2^2 + (−2)^2] = √[4 + 4] = √8 = 2√2 units

ii. P(−5, 7), Q(−1, 3)  
x2 − x1 = −1 − (−5) = 4,  y2 − y1 = 3 − 7 = −4  
d = √[4^2 + (−4)^2] = √[16 + 16] = √32 = 4√2 units

iii. R(0, −3), S(0, 5/2)  
x2 − x1 = 0 − 0 = 0,  y2 − y1 = 5/2 − (−3) = 5/2 + 3 = 11/2  
d = √[0^2 + (11/2)^2] = |11/2| = 11/2 units

iv. L(5, −8), M(−7, −3)  
x2 − x1 = −7 − 5 = −12,  y2 − y1 = −3 − (−8) = 5  
d = √[(−12)^2 + 5^2] = √[144 + 25] = √169 = 13 units

v. T(−3, 6), R(9, −10)  
x2 − x1 = 9 − (−3) = 12,  y2 − y1 = −10 − 6 = −16  
d = √[12^2 + (−16)^2] = √[144 + 256] = √400 = 20 units

vi. W(−7/2, 4), X(11, 4)  
x2 − x1 = 11 − (−7/2) = 11 + 7/2 = 22/2 + 7/2 = 29/2,  y2 − y1 = 4 − 4 = 0  
d = √[(29/2)^2 + 0^2] = 29/2 units

Final answer

i. 2√2 units  
ii. 4√2 units  
iii. 11/2 units  
iv. 13 units  
v. 20 units  
vi. 29/2 units

Question 2  
Determine whether the points are collinear.

i. A(1, −3), B(2, −5), C(−4, 7)  
ii. L(−2, 3), M(1, −3), N(5, 4)  
iii. R(0, 3), D(2, 1), S(3, −1)  
iv. P(−2, 3), Q(1, 2), R(4, 1)

Method  
Use the slope criterion: three points are collinear if the slope between one pair equals the slope between another pair. For two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), slope = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1). If slopes are equal (and defined), the points lie on the same straight line.

Working

i. A(1, −3), B(2, −5), C(−4, 7)  
Slope AB = (−5 − (−3)) / (2 − 1) = (−2)/1 = −2.  
Slope AC = (7 − (−3)) / (−4 − 1) = 10/(−5) = −2.  
Since slope AB = slope AC = −2, A, B and C are collinear.

ii. L(−2, 3), M(1, −3), N(5, 4)  
Slope LM = (−3 − 3) / (1 − (−2)) = (−6)/3 = −2.  
Slope LN = (4 − 3) / (5 − (−2)) = 1/7.  
Slopes differ (−2 ≠ 1/7), so L, M and N are not collinear.

iii. R(0, 3), D(2, 1), S(3, −1)  
Slope RD = (1 − 3) / (2 − 0) = (−2)/2 = −1.  
Slope RS = (−1 − 3) / (3 − 0) = (−4)/3.  
Slopes differ (−1 ≠ −4/3), so R, D and S are not collinear.

iv. P(−2, 3), Q(1, 2), R(4, 1)  
Slope PQ = (2 − 3) / (1 − (−2)) = (−1)/3 = −1/3.  
Slope QR = (1 − 2) / (4 − 1) = (−1)/3 = −1/3.  
Slopes are equal, so P, Q and R are collinear.

(Additional check for part iv: distances)  
PQ = sqrt[(1 − (−2))^2 + (2 − 3)^2] = sqrt[3^2 + (−1)^2] = sqrt(10).  
QR = sqrt[(4 − 1)^2 + (1 − 2)^2] = sqrt[3^2 + (−1)^2] = sqrt(10).  
PR = sqrt[(4 − (−2))^2 + (1 − 3)^2] = sqrt[6^2 + (−2)^2] = sqrt(40) = 2·sqrt(10).  
PQ + QR = sqrt(10) + sqrt(10) = 2·sqrt(10) = PR, confirming Q lies between P and R.

Final answer
i. Collinear.  
ii. Not collinear.  
iii. Not collinear.  
iv. Collinear.

Question
Find the point on the X-axis which is equidistant from A(−3, 4) and B(1, −4).

Method
A point on the X-axis has y-coordinate 0. Let the required point be C(x, 0). Use the distance formula AC = BC, square both sides to remove square roots, and solve for x. Verify the result.

Working
Let C(x, 0).

Distance AC = sqrt[(x − (−3))^2 + (0 − 4)^2] = sqrt[(x + 3)^2 + (−4)^2] = sqrt[(x + 3)^2 + 16].

Distance BC = sqrt[(x − 1)^2 + (0 − (−4))^2] = sqrt[(x − 1)^2 + 4^2] = sqrt[(x − 1)^2 + 16].

Set AC = BC:
(x + 3)^2 + 16 = (x − 1)^2 + 16.

Subtract 16 from both sides:
(x + 3)^2 = (x − 1)^2.

Expand both sides:
x^2 + 6x + 9 = x^2 − 2x + 1.

Cancel x^2 and collect like terms:
6x + 9 = −2x + 1
8x = −8
x = −1.

Verify:
AC = sqrt[(−1 + 3)^2 + (−4)^2] = sqrt[2^2 + 16] = sqrt[4 + 16] = sqrt20.
BC = sqrt[(−1 − 1)^2 + 4^2] = sqrt[(−2)^2 + 16] = sqrt[4 + 16] = sqrt20.
AC = BC, so C is correct.

Final answer
The point on the X-axis equidistant from A and B is (−1, 0).

Question
Verify that the points P(−2, 2), Q(2, 2) and R(2, 7) are vertices of a right‑angled triangle.

Method
Use the distance formula to find the squares of the three side lengths:
distance squared between (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is (x2−x1)^2 + (y2−y1)^2.
If the sum of the squares of two sides equals the square of the third side, the triangle is right‑angled (converse of Pythagoras). Optionally, check slopes to identify which angle is right.

Diagram cue
A diagram is supplied in the text. All necessary numeric information is given by the coordinates; no additional diagram data is required.

Working
1. Compute PQ^2:
   PQ^2 = (2 − (−2))^2 + (2 − 2)^2
        = (4)^2 + 0^2
        = 16.

2. Compute QR^2:
   QR^2 = (2 − 2)^2 + (7 − 2)^2
        = 0^2 + (5)^2
        = 25.

3. Compute PR^2:
   PR^2 = (2 − (−2))^2 + (7 − 2)^2
        = (4)^2 + (5)^2
        = 16 + 25
        = 41.

4. Compare:
   PQ^2 + QR^2 = 16 + 25 = 41 = PR^2.

   Therefore PQ^2 + QR^2 = PR^2, so by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem the triangle PQR is right‑angled. Since PR is the longest side (√41), it is the hypotenuse and the right angle is at Q.

(Alternative quick check by slopes: slope of PQ = (2−2)/(2−(−2)) = 0 (horizontal); slope of QR = (7−2)/(2−2) = undefined (vertical). A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line, so angle at Q is 90°.)

Final answer
Points P(−2, 2), Q(2, 2) and R(2, 7) are vertices of a right‑angled triangle. The right angle is at Q.

Question  
Show that points P(2, −2), Q(7, 3), R(11, −1) and S(6, −6) are vertices of a parallelogram.

Method  
We will compute slopes and lengths of opposite sides. If each pair of opposite sides is parallel (same slope) and equal in length, the quadrilateral PQRS is a parallelogram.

Working

1. Compute slope and length of PQ:
- Slope PQ = (y_Q − y_P) / (x_Q − x_P) = (3 − (−2)) / (7 − 2) = 5 / 5 = 1.
- Length PQ = √[(7 − 2)^2 + (3 − (−2))^2] = √(25 + 25) = √50 = 5√2.

2. Compute slope and length of RS:
- Slope RS = (y_S − y_R) / (x_S − x_R) = (−6 − (−1)) / (6 − 11) = (−5) / (−5) = 1.
- Length RS = √[(6 − 11)^2 + (−6 − (−1))^2] = √(25 + 25) = √50 = 5√2.

Conclusion for one pair: PQ and RS have the same slope (1) and equal lengths (5√2), so PQ ∥ RS and PQ = RS.

3. Compute slope and length of QR:
- Slope QR = (y_R − y_Q) / (x_R − x_Q) = (−1 − 3) / (11 − 7) = (−4) / 4 = −1.
- Length QR = √[(11 − 7)^2 + (−1 − 3)^2] = √(16 + 16) = √32 = 4√2.

4. Compute slope and length of PS:
- Slope PS = (y_S − y_P) / (x_S − x_P) = (−6 − (−2)) / (6 − 2) = (−4) / 4 = −1.
- Length PS = √[(6 − 2)^2 + (−6 − (−2))^2] = √(16 + 16) = √32 = 4√2.

Conclusion for other pair: QR and PS have the same slope (−1) and equal lengths (4√2), so QR ∥ PS and QR = PS.

Final answer  
Both pairs of opposite sides of quadrilateral PQRS are parallel and equal in length. Therefore PQRS is a parallelogram. Hence the points P(2, −2), Q(7, 3), R(11, −1) and S(6, −6) are vertices of a parallelogram.

Question
Show that points A (−4, −7), B (−1, 2), C (8, 5) and D (5, −4) are vertices of rhombus ABCD.

Method
Use the distance formula to compute the lengths of the four sides AB, BC, CD and DA. If all four side lengths are equal and the quadrilateral is non‑degenerate (area ≠ 0), then by definition the quadrilateral is a rhombus.

Working
Distance formula: distance between (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is sqrt[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2].

1. AB:
Vector B − A = (−1 − (−4), 2 − (−7)) = (3, 9).
AB = sqrt(3^2 + 9^2) = sqrt(9 + 81) = sqrt(90) = 3√10.

2. BC:
Vector C − B = (8 − (−1), 5 − 2) = (9, 3).
BC = sqrt(9^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(81 + 9) = sqrt(90) = 3√10.

3. CD:
Vector D − C = (5 − 8, −4 − 5) = (−3, −9).
CD = sqrt((−3)^2 + (−9)^2) = sqrt(9 + 81) = sqrt(90) = 3√10.

4. DA:
Vector A − D = (−4 − 5, −7 − (−4)) = (−9, −3).
DA = sqrt((−9)^2 + (−3)^2) = sqrt(81 + 9) = sqrt(90) = 3√10.

All four sides are equal: AB = BC = CD = DA = 3√10.

Check quadrilateral is non‑degenerate (area ≠ 0) using the shoelace formula:
Using order A(−4,−7), B(−1,2), C(8,5), D(5,−4),

sum1 = (−4)(2) + (−1)(5) + 8(−4) + 5(−7) = −8 − 5 − 32 − 35 = −80.
sum2 = (−7)(−1) + 2·8 + 5·5 + (−4)(−4) = 7 + 16 + 25 + 16 = 64.
Area = (1/2)|sum1 − sum2| = (1/2)|−80 − 64| = (1/2)·144 = 72 ≠ 0.

Since all four sides are equal and the quadrilateral is non‑degenerate, ABCD is a rhombus.

Final answer
AB = BC = CD = DA = 3√10, area = 72; therefore ABCD is a rhombus.

Question
Find x if the distance between points L(x, 7) and M(1, 15) is 10.

Method
Use the distance formula for two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
distance = sqrt[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2].
Substitute the given coordinates and solve for x.

Diagram cue
A diagram may show the two points, but it gives no extra numerical information beyond the coordinates. All needed work uses the coordinates and the distance formula.

Working
Let L(x1, y1) = (x, 7) and M(x2, y2) = (1, 15).
Distance LM = 10, so
sqrt[(1 − x)^2 + (15 − 7)^2] = 10.

Compute the y-difference squared: (15 − 7)^2 = 8^2 = 64.
So sqrt[(1 − x)^2 + 64] = 10.
Square both sides: (1 − x)^2 + 64 = 100.
Thus (1 − x)^2 = 36.
Take square roots: 1 − x = 6 or 1 − x = −6.

Solve each case:
If 1 − x = 6, then x = 1 − 6 = −5.
If 1 − x = −6, then x = 1 + 6 = 7.

Final answer
x = −5 or x = 7.

Question  
Show that the points A(1, 2), B(1, 6), C(1 + 2√3, 4) are vertices of an equilateral triangle.

Method  
Use the distance formula to find AB, BC and AC. If all three distances are equal, the triangle is equilateral.

Working
- Distance formula: for P(x1,y1) and Q(x2,y2), PQ = √[(x2−x1)^2 + (y2−y1)^2].

1. AB:
  - A(1,2), B(1,6) ⇒ dx = 1−1 = 0, dy = 6−2 = 4
  - AB = √[0^2 + 4^2] = √16 = 4

2. AC:
  - A(1,2), C(1 + 2√3, 4) ⇒ dx = (1 + 2√3) − 1 = 2√3, dy = 4 − 2 = 2
  - AC = √[(2√3)^2 + 2^2] = √[4·3 + 4] = √[12 + 4] = √16 = 4

3. BC:
  - B(1,6), C(1 + 2√3, 4) ⇒ dx = (1 + 2√3) − 1 = 2√3, dy = 4 − 6 = −2
  - BC = √[(2√3)^2 + (−2)^2] = √[12 + 4] = √16 = 4

All three sides AB, AC and BC equal 4.

Final answer  
Since AB = BC = AC = 4, triangle ABC has three equal sides and therefore is an equilateral triangle. Hence A, B and C are vertices of an equilateral triangle.

Question  
Find the coordinates of point P if P divides the line segment joining A(−1, 7) and B(4, −3) in the ratio 2 : 3.

Method  
If a point P divides the segment AB internally in the ratio AP : PB = m : n, with A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2), then
x-coordinate of P = (m x2 + n x1) / (m + n),
y-coordinate of P = (m y2 + n y1) / (m + n).
(These come from writing P as A + (m/(m+n))(B − A).)

Working  
Here A(−1, 7), B(4, −3) and AP : PB = 2 : 3, so m = 2, n = 3.

xP = (m x2 + n x1) / (m + n) = (2·4 + 3·(−1)) / 5 = (8 − 3) / 5 = 5 / 5 = 1.  
yP = (m y2 + n y1) / (m + n) = (2·(−3) + 3·7) / 5 = (−6 + 21) / 5 = 15 / 5 = 3.

Final answer  
P = (1, 3).

Method

x_A = (b·x1 + a·x2)/(a + b),  y_A = (b·y1 + a·y2)/(a + b).
(This is a weighted average of the endpoint coordinates, weights being the parts of the opposite segment.)

Working

i. P(−3, 7), Q(1, −4), a = 2, b = 1  
x_A = (b·x1 + a·x2)/(a + b) = (1·(−3) + 2·1)/(2 + 1) = (−3 + 2)/3 = −1/3

y_A = (2·6 + 1·1)/3 = (12 + 1)/3 = 13/3

Question  
Find the ratio in which point T(-1, 6) divides the line segment joining P(-3, 10) and Q(6, -8).

Method  
Use the section formula. If a point T divides PQ internally in the ratio m:n (that is, PT:TQ = m:n), then
x_T = (n·x_P + m·x_Q) / (m + n),  y_T = (n·y_P + m·y_Q) / (m + n).
We substitute P = (x1,y1) = (-3,10), Q = (x2,y2) = (6,-8), T = (x,y) = (-1,6) and solve for m:n.

Working
1. Apply the x-coordinate relation:
   -1 = (n·(-3) + m·6) / (m + n)
   Multiply both sides by (m + n):
   -1(m + n) = -3n + 6m
   => -m - n = -3n + 6m
   => bring terms together: -m - n + 3n - 6m = 0
   => -7m + 2n = 0
   => 2n = 7m  ---> (1)

2. Apply the y-coordinate relation:
   6 = (n·10 + m·(-8)) / (m + n)
   Multiply both sides by (m + n):
   6(m + n) = 10n - 8m
   => 6m + 6n = 10n - 8m
   => 6m + 6n - 10n + 8m = 0
   => 14m - 4n = 0
   => 4n = 14m  ---> (2)

3. Compare (1) and (2):
   From (1): 2n = 7m  => n = (7/2)m
   From (2): 4n = 14m => n = (14/4)m = (7/2)m
   Both give the same relation, so m:n = 2:7.

Final answer  
T divides the segment PQ internally in the ratio PT:TQ = 2 : 7.

Question  
Point P is the centre of the circle and AB is a diameter. Find the coordinates of point B if coordinates of point A and P are (2, -3) and (-2, 0) respectively.

Method  
The centre of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter. So P is the midpoint of segment AB. Use the midpoint formula: if A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2), then midpoint M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). Put M = P and solve for x2 and y2.

Working  
Let A = (x1, y1) = (2, −3), P = (x, y) = (−2, 0), and B = (x2, y2).  
From midpoint formula:
(x1 + x2)/2 = x  and  (y1 + y2)/2 = y.

Substitute values:
(2 + x2)/2 = −2  ⇒  2 + x2 = −4  ⇒  x2 = −4 − 2 = −6.
(−3 + y2)/2 = 0  ⇒  −3 + y2 = 0  ⇒  y2 = 3.

Final answer  
B = (−6, 3)

Question
Find the ratio in which point P(k, 7) divides the segment joining A(8, 9) and B(1, 2). Also find k.

Method
Use the section formula for internal division. If P divides AB in the ratio AP:PB = m:n (internal), then
x-coordinate of P = (n·xA + m·xB) / (m + n),
y-coordinate of P = (n·yA + m·yB) / (m + n).
Here A(8,9), B(1,2), P(k,7). Use the y-coordinate to find m:n, then use that ratio in the x-coordinate to find k.

Working
Let AP:PB = m:n.

From the y-coordinate:
7 = (n·9 + m·2) / (m + n)
Multiply both sides by (m + n):
7(m + n) = 9n + 2m
7m + 7n = 9n + 2m
Bring like terms together:
7m − 2m = 9n − 7n
5m = 2n
Thus m:n = 2:5. So AP:PB = 2:5 (internal division).

Now use the x-coordinate to find k:
k = (n·xA + m·xB) / (m + n) = (5·8 + 2·1) / (2 + 5) = (40 + 2) / 7 = 42 / 7 = 6.

Final answer
P divides AB internally in the ratio AP:PB = 2:5, and k = 6.

Question
Find the coordinates of the points of trisection of the line segment AB with A(2, 7) and B(−4, −8).

Method
A point that trisects AB lies on AB at a fractional distance from A toward B. If a point lies at fraction t of the way from A to B (t = 1/3 or 2/3 for trisection), its coordinates are
(x, y) = A + t(B − A) = (x_A + t(x_B − x_A), y_A + t(y_B − y_A)).
(Using the vector/section approach avoids sign confusion.)

Working
1. Compute the vector B − A:
   B − A = (−4 − 2, −8 − 7) = (−6, −15).

2. First trisection point P is 1/3 of the way from A to B (t = 1/3):
   P = A + (1/3)(B − A)
     = (2, 7) + (1/3)(−6, −15)
     = (2 + (−6)/3, 7 + (−15)/3)
     = (2 − 2, 7 − 5)
     = (0, 2).

3. Second trisection point Q is 2/3 of the way from A to B (t = 2/3):
   Q = A + (2/3)(B − A)
     = (2, 7) + (2/3)(−6, −15)
     = (2 + (−12)/3, 7 + (−30)/3)
     = (2 − 4, 7 − 10)
     = (−2, −3).

Final answer
The coordinates of the points of trisection of AB are P(0, 2) and Q(−2, −3).

Diagram cue
The textbook diagram is not needed for numerical computation; no additional lengths or labels are required.

If A(-14, -10), B(6, -2) are given, find the coordinates of the points which divide segment AB into four equal parts.

Use the vector/section idea: the vector from A to B is AB = B − A. Dividing AB into four equal parts gives a step vector AB/4. Starting from A and adding this step repeatedly gives the three interior points that divide AB into four equal segments. (Equivalently, these points lie at 1/4, 2/4 and 3/4 of the way from A to B.)

Working
1. Compute vector AB:
   AB = (6 − (−14), −2 − (−10)) = (20, 8).

2. One quarter of AB (the step) is:
   AB/4 = (20/4, 8/4) = (5, 2).

3. Points dividing AB into four equal parts:
   - Point C (1/4 from A): A + AB/4 = (−14 + 5, −10 + 2) = (−9, −8).
   - Point D (2/4 = midpoint): A + 2·(AB/4) = (−14 + 10, −10 + 4) = (−4, −6).
   - Point E (3/4 from A): A + 3·(AB/4) = (−14 + 15, −10 + 6) = (1, −4).

Final answer  
The coordinates of the points that divide segment AB into four equal parts are:
C(−9, −8), D(−4, −6), E(1, −4).

Question  
A(15, 5), B(9, 20) and A–P–B. Find the ratio in which point P(11, 15) divides segment AB. Find the ratio using x and y co‑ordinates. Write the conclusion.

Method  
Let AP : PB = m : n (point P divides AB internally). Using the section (or weighted-average) formula: if P divides A(x1,y1) and B(x2,y2) in the ratio m:n (AP:PB = m:n), then
P = ((n x1 + m x2)/(m + n), (n y1 + m y2)/(m + n)).
Use the x‑coordinate and y‑coordinate equations to find m:n.

Diagram cue  
A diagram is mentioned in the book. No extra numerical information from the diagram is needed; we use only the given coordinates.

Working
Let A(15,5) = (x1,y1), B(9,20) = (x2,y2), and AP:PB = m:n. According to the section formula,
x-coordinate of P:
(15n + 9m)/(m + n) = 11.

Multiply both sides by (m + n):
15n + 9m = 11m + 11n
Rearrange:
15n − 11n + 9m − 11m = 0
4n − 2m = 0
2n − m = 0
So m = 2n.

y-coordinate of P:
(5n + 20m)/(m + n) = 15.

Multiply both sides by (m + n):
5n + 20m = 15m + 15n
Rearrange:
5n − 15n + 20m − 15m = 0
−10n + 5m = 0
5m − 10n = 0
So m = 2n.

Both coordinates give the same relation m = 2n. Therefore AP:PB = m:n = 2n : n = 2 : 1.

Final answer  
Point P(11,15) divides segment AB internally in the ratio AP : PB = 2 : 1. The ratio obtained from the x‑coordinate and from the y‑coordinate are the same.

Question
Suppose point R divides segment PQ externally in the ratio 3 : 1. Show that Q divides PR internally in the ratio 2 : 1. If P = (x1, y1) and Q = (x2, y2), find the coordinates of R.

Method
Use a parameter (section) representation of a point on line PQ. Represent R as P + t(Q − P). Determine t from the given ratio PR : QR = 3 : 1, then (a) deduce the internal ratio in which Q divides PR and (b) find R’s coordinates by substituting t.

Working
1. Collinearity and parameter form
- Let position vectors (or coordinates) be P = (x1, y1), Q = (x2, y2).
- Any point R on the line through P and Q can be written as
  R = P + t(Q − P) for some scalar t.
  So coordinates of R are ((1 − t)x1 + t x2, (1 − t)y1 + t y2).

2. Relate t to the ratio PR : QR
- The directed segment lengths along the line satisfy
  PR = |t| · |Q − P| and QR = |t − 1| · |Q − P|.
- For R beyond Q (external division with order P — Q — R), t > 1, and the ratio
  PR / QR = t / (t − 1).
- Given PR : QR = 3 : 1, we have
  t / (t − 1) = 3 / 1.
- Solve for t:
  t = 3(t − 1)  ⇒  t = 3t − 3  ⇒  2t = 3  ⇒  t = 3/2.

3. Show Q divides PR internally in ratio 2 : 1
- With t = 3/2, compute PQ length in units of common part k:
  PR = t · |Q − P| = (3/2)|Q − P|, QR = (t − 1)|Q − P| = (1/2)|Q − P|.
  Thus PR : QR = (3/2) : (1/2) = 3 : 1 (consistent).
- PQ = PR − QR = (3/2 − 1/2)|Q − P| = (2/2)|Q − P| = 1·|Q − P|.
  So PQ : QR = 1 : (1/2) = 2 : 1.
- Therefore Q divides the segment PR internally in the ratio PQ : QR = 2 : 1.

4. Coordinates of R (special case m = 3, n = 1)
- Using t = 3/2 in R = ((1 − t)x1 + t x2, (1 − t)y1 + t y2):
  1 − t = 1 − 3/2 = −1/2.
- Hence
  x_R = (−1/2)x1 + (3/2)x2 = (−x1 + 3x2)/2,
  y_R = (−1/2)y1 + (3/2)y2 = (−y1 + 3y2)/2.

(For reference, the general external section formula: if PR : RQ = m : n, then
R = ( (−n x1 + m x2)/(m − n), (−n y1 + m y2)/(m − n) ).)

Diagram cue
The textbook diagram indicates R lies on the extension of PQ beyond Q (order P — Q — R). No additional lengths are assumed from the diagram.

Final answer
- Q divides PR internally in the ratio 2 : 1.
- If P = (x1, y1) and Q = (x2, y2) and R divides PQ externally in the ratio 3 : 1, then
  R = ( (−x1 + 3x2)/2 , (−y1 + 3y2)/2 ).

Question
- The angles made by a line with the positive direction of the x-axis are:
  i. 45°
  ii. 60°
  iii. 90°
  Find the slope of each line.

Method
- For a line that makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis, its slope m is given by m = tan θ.
- Evaluate tan θ for each given angle. If tan θ is not defined (division by zero), the slope is undefined and the line is vertical.

Working
i) θ = 45°
- m = tan 45°.
- tan 45° = 1.
- Hence m = 1.

ii) θ = 60°
- m = tan 60°.
- tan 60° = √3.
- Hence m = √3.

iii) θ = 90°
- m = tan 90°.
- tan 90° involves division by cos 90°, and cos 90° = 0, so tan 90° is not defined.
- A line making 90° with the positive x-axis is vertical; vertical lines do not have a finite slope.

Final answer
i. m = 1
ii. m = √3
iii. m is undefined (the line is vertical)

Question
Determine whether the following points are collinear.

i. A(−1, −1), B(0, 1), C(1, 3)  
ii. D(−2, −3), E(1, 0), F(2, 1)  
iii. L(2, 5), M(3, 3), N(5, 1)  
iv. P(2, −5), Q(1, −3), R(−2, 3)  
v. R(1, −4), S(−2, 2), T(−3, 4)  
vi. A(−4, 4), K[−2, 5 2], N(4, −2)

Method
Three points (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (x3,y3) are collinear if the slope between the first two equals the slope between the last two:
slope = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1).  
Equivalently, the area (determinant) test: x1(y2 − y3) + x2(y3 − y1) + x3(y1 − y2) = 0.

Working
i. A(−1,−1), B(0,1), C(1,3)
- slope AB = (1 − (−1)) / (0 − (−1)) = 2 / 1 = 2
- slope BC = (3 − 1) / (1 − 0) = 2 / 1 = 2
Since slopes are equal, A, B, C are collinear.

ii. D(−2,−3), E(1,0), F(2,1)
- slope DE = (0 − (−3)) / (1 − (−2)) = 3 / 3 = 1
- slope EF = (1 − 0) / (2 − 1) = 1 / 1 = 1
Slopes equal → D, E, F are collinear.

iii. L(2,5), M(3,3), N(5,1)
- slope LM = (3 − 5) / (3 − 2) = −2 / 1 = −2
- slope MN = (1 − 3) / (5 − 3) = −2 / 2 = −1
Slopes are different → L, M, N are not collinear.

iv. P(2,−5), Q(1,−3), R(−2,3)
- slope PQ = (−3 − (−5)) / (1 − 2) = 2 / (−1) = −2
- slope QR = (3 − (−3)) / (−2 − 1) = 6 / (−3) = −2
Slopes equal → P, Q, R are collinear.

v. R(1,−4), S(−2,2), T(−3,4)
- slope RS = (2 − (−4)) / (−2 − 1) = 6 / (−3) = −2
- slope ST = (4 − 2) / (−3 − (−2)) = 2 / (−1) = −2
Slopes equal → R, S, T are collinear.

vi. A(−4,4), K[−2,5 2], N(4,−2)
Diagram cue: The coordinate written for K in the question is ambiguous ("K[−2,5 2]"). Do not assume an interpretation not given. Use the general collinearity condition for A(−4,4), K(h,k), N(4,−2):

Using the determinant test:
x1(y2 − y3) + x2(y3 − y1) + x3(y1 − y2) = 0
Plugging A(−4,4), K(h,k), N(4,−2):
(−4)(k − (−2)) + h((−2) − 4) + 4(4 − k) = 0
Simplify:
−4(k + 2) − 6h + 16 − 4k = 0
⇒ −6h − 8k + 8 = 0
⇒ 3h + 4k = 4.

So K must satisfy 3x + 4y = 4 to lie on the line through A and N.
- If K = (−2, 5/2) then 3(−2) + 4(5/2) = −6 + 10 = 4 → K lies on the line and A, K, N are collinear.
- If K = (−2, 5) then 3(−2) + 4(5) = −6 + 20 = 14 ≠ 4 → not collinear.
Because the given K is unclear, we cannot decide numerically without the correct coordinates. The required condition for K to make A, K, N collinear is 3x + 4y = 4.

iv. Collinear

Question  
If A(1, −1), B(0, 4), C(−5, 3) are vertices of a triangle, find the slope of each side AB, BC and AC.

Method  
Slope of a line through two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is given by (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1). Apply this formula to each pair of vertices.

Working
1. Slope of AB (points A(1, −1) and B(0, 4)):
   m_AB = (y_B − y_A) / (x_B − x_A) = (4 − (−1)) / (0 − 1) = 5 / (−1) = −5.

2. Slope of BC (points B(0, 4) and C(−5, 3)):
   m_BC = (y_C − y_B) / (x_C − x_B) = (3 − 4) / (−5 − 0) = (−1) / (−5) = 1/5.

3. Slope of AC (points A(1, −1) and C(−5, 3)):
   m_AC = (y_C − y_A) / (x_C − x_A) = (3 − (−1)) / (−5 − 1) = 4 / (−6) = −2/3.

Final answer
- Slope of AB = −5  
- Slope of BC = 1/5  
- Slope of AC = −2/3

Question
A(-4, -7), B(-1, 2), C(8, 5) and D(5, -4) are four points. Show that these are the vertices of a parallelogram.

Given
A(−4, −7), B(−1, 2), C(8, 5), D(5, −4)

To prove
Quadrilateral ABCD is a parallelogram.

Proof / Steps
1. Compute the slope of AB.
   slope AB = (y_B − y_A) / (x_B − x_A)
            = (2 − (−7)) / (−1 − (−4))
            = 9 / 3
            = 3.

2. Compute the slope of CD.
   slope CD = (y_C − y_D) / (x_C − x_D)
            = (5 − (−4)) / (8 − 5)
            = 9 / 3
            = 3.

   Since slope AB = slope CD, AB ∥ CD.

3. Compute the slope of BC.
   slope BC = (y_C − y_B) / (x_C − x_B)
            = (5 − 2) / (8 − (−1))
            = 3 / 9
            = 1/3.

4. Compute the slope of AD.
   slope AD = (y_D − y_A) / (x_D − x_A)
            = (−4 − (−7)) / (5 − (−4))
            = 3 / 9
            = 1/3.

   Since slope BC = slope AD, BC ∥ AD.

5. A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Here AB ∥ CD and BC ∥ AD, and the four points are distinct, so ABCD is a parallelogram.

Result
ABCD is a parallelogram; hence the points A(−4, −7), B(−1, 2), C(8, 5) and D(5, −4) are the vertices of a parallelogram.

Question  
Find k, if R(1, −1), S(−2, k) and slope of line RS is −2.

Method  
Use the slope formula for two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):  
slope m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1).  
Substitute the coordinates of R and S and the given slope, then solve for k.

Diagram cue  
A diagram is mentioned in the book, but all needed information is given by the coordinates and the slope. No additional diagram measurements are required.

Working  
Let R = (1, −1) and S = (−2, k). Using the slope formula:
m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1) = (k − (−1)) / (−2 − 1) = (k + 1) / (−3).

Given m = −2, so
(k + 1) / (−3) = −2.

Multiply both sides by −3:
k + 1 = (−2)(−3) = 6.

Therefore k = 6 − 1 = 5.

(Check) For k = 5, slope = (5 − (−1)) / (−2 − 1) = 6 / (−3) = −2, which matches the given slope.

Final answer  
k = 5.

Find k, if B(k, −5), C(1, 2) and the slope of line BC is 7.

Method  
Use the slope formula for two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): m = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1).

Working  
Let B(k, −5) be (x1, y1) and C(1, 2) be (x2, y2).  
So y2 − y1 = 2 − (−5) = 7, and x2 − x1 = 1 − k.  
Slope m = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1) = 7/(1 − k).  
Given slope m = 7, so 7/(1 − k) = 7.  
Since the slope is finite, 1 − k ≠ 0. Divide both sides by 7: 1/(1 − k) = 1.  
Thus 1 − k = 1, which gives k = 0.

Question  
Find k if PQ ∥ RS and P(2, 4), Q(3, 6), R(3, 1), S(5, k).

Method  
If two lines are parallel, their slopes are equal. Compute slope of PQ and set it equal to slope of RS, then solve for k.

Working
1. Slope of PQ = (y_Q − y_P) / (x_Q − x_P)  
   = (6 − 4) / (3 − 2) = 2 / 1 = 2.

2. Slope of RS = (y_S − y_R) / (x_S − x_R)  
   = (k − 1) / (5 − 3) = (k − 1) / 2.

3. Set slopes equal (since PQ ∥ RS):  
   2 = (k − 1) / 2.

4. Multiply both sides by 2:  
   4 = k − 1.

5. Solve for k:  
   k = 4 + 1 = 5.

Final answer  
k = 5.

Question  
Fill in the blanks using correct alternatives.

i. Segment AB is parallel to Y-axis and coordinates of point A are (1, 3). Then coordinates of point B can be _______.  
Options: (A) (3,1)  (B) (5,3)  (C) (3,0)  (D) (1,-3)

ii. Out of the following, point that lies to the right of the origin on X-axis is _______.  
Options: (A) (-2,0)  (B) (0,2)  (C) (2,3)  (D) (2,0)

iii. Distance of point (-3, 4) from the origin is _________.  
Options: (A) 7  (B) 1  (C) 5  (D) -5

iv. A line makes an angle of 30° with the positive direction of X-axis. So the slope of the line is ________.  
Options: (A) 1/2  (B) 3√2  (C) 1/√3  (D) √3

Method  
- If a segment is parallel to the y-axis, all points on it have the same x-coordinate.  
- A point lies on the positive x-axis if its y-coordinate is 0 and its x-coordinate is positive.  
- Distance from origin to (x, y) = √(x^2 + y^2).  
- Slope of a line making angle θ with positive x-axis = tan θ.

Working
i. A = (1, 3). For AB || y-axis, x-coordinate of B must equal 1. Among the options only (1, −3) has x = 1. So B = (1, −3).

ii. Point on positive x-axis must have form (x, 0) with x > 0. Check options: (-2,0) has x < 0; (0,2) not on x-axis; (2,3) not on x-axis; (2,0) fits. So (2,0).

iii. Distance from origin to (−3, 4) = √[ (−3)^2 + 4^2 ] = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

iv. Slope = tan(30°). tan 30° = 1/√3. So slope = 1/√3.

Final answer
i. (D) (1, −3)  
ii. (D) (2, 0)  
iii. (C) 5  
iv. (C) 1/√3

Question  
Determine whether the given points are collinear.

i. A(0, 2), B(1, −0.5), C(2, −3)  
ii. P(1, 2), Q(2, 8/5), R(3, 6/5)  
iii. L(1, 2), M(5, 3), N(8, 6)

Method  
Three points are collinear if the slope of one segment equals the slope of the adjacent segment with the common point. For points (x1,y1), (x2,y2) and (x3,y3) with the middle point (x2,y2), compute slope12 = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1) and slope23 = (y3 − y2)/(x3 − x2). If slope12 = slope23, the points are collinear.

Working

i. A(0, 2), B(1, −0.5), C(2, −3)  
- Slope AB = (yB − yA)/(xB − xA) = (−0.5 − 2)/(1 − 0) = (−2.5)/1 = −5/2.  
  (Using fractions: −0.5 = −1/2, so (−1/2 − 2) = (−1/2 − 4/2) = −5/2.)  
- Slope BC = (yC − yB)/(xC − xB) = (−3 − (−0.5))/(2 − 1) = (−2.5)/1 = −5/2.  
Since slope AB = slope BC (both −5/2), A, B, C are collinear.

ii. P(1, 2), Q(2, 8/5), R(3, 6/5)  
- Slope PQ = (yQ − yP)/(xQ − xP) = (8/5 − 2)/(2 − 1) = (8/5 − 10/5)/1 = (−2/5).  
- Slope QR = (yR − yQ)/(xR − xQ) = (6/5 − 8/5)/(3 − 2) = (−2/5)/1 = (−2/5).  
Since slope PQ = slope QR (both −2/5), P, Q, R are collinear.

iii. L(1, 2), M(5, 3), N(8, 6)  
- Slope LM = (yM − yL)/(xM − xL) = (3 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 1/4.  
- Slope MN = (yN − yM)/(xN − xM) = (6 − 3)/(8 − 5) = 3/3 = 1.  
Since slope LM (1/4) ≠ slope MN (1), L, M, N are not collinear.

Final answer
i. A, B, C are collinear.  
ii. P, Q, R are collinear.  
iii. L, M, N are not collinear.

Question
Find the coordinates of the midpoint of the line segment joining P(0, 6) and Q(12, 20).

Method
The midpoint M of a segment with endpoints (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is found by averaging the x-coordinates and averaging the y-coordinates:
M = ( (x1 + x2)/2 , (y1 + y2)/2 ).

Diagram cue: If the book shows a diagram of PQ, it only illustrates the segment; no additional numerical values are needed beyond the given coordinates.

Working
Let P = (x1, y1) = (0, 6) and Q = (x2, y2) = (12, 20).

Compute the x-coordinate of the midpoint:
(x1 + x2)/2 = (0 + 12)/2 = 12/2 = 6.

Compute the y-coordinate of the midpoint:
(y1 + y2)/2 = (6 + 20)/2 = 26/2 = 13.

Final answer
The midpoint of PQ is (6, 13).

Question  
Find the ratio in which the line segment joining the points A(3, 8) and B(−9, 3) is divided by the Y-axis.

Method  
Let C be the point where the Y-axis (x = 0) meets segment AB. If AC : CB = m : n (internal division), use the section formula for internal division:
C = ( (n x1 + m x2)/(m + n), (n y1 + m y2)/(m + n) ),
where A = (x1, y1) and B = (x2, y2). Set the x-coordinate of C equal to 0 and solve for the ratio m : n.

Working  
A = (3, 8) so x1 = 3, y1 = 8.  
B = (−9, 3) so x2 = −9, y2 = 3.  
Let AC : CB = m : n. Then the x-coordinate of C is
0 = (n·x1 + m·x2) / (m + n) = (3n + (−9)m)/(m + n).
Thus 3n − 9m = 0 ⇒ n = 3m.

So AC : CB = m : n = m : 3m = 1 : 3.

For completeness, the y-coordinate of C is
y = (n·y1 + m·y2)/(m + n) = (3m·8 + m·3)/(4m) = (24m + 3m)/(4m) = 27/4.
Hence C = (0, 27/4).

Final answer  
The Y-axis divides the segment AB internally in the ratio 1 : 3 (AC : CB = 1 : 3). The point of division is C(0, 27/4).

Question 5

Find the point on the x-axis which is equidistant from P(2, −5) and Q(−2, 9).

Method

A point on the x-axis has y-coordinate 0. Let R = (x, 0). Equate squared distances PR^2 and QR^2 and solve for x.

Working

PR^2 = (x − 2)^2 + (0 − (−5))^2 = (x − 2)^2 + 5^2 = (x − 2)^2 + 25.

QR^2 = (x − (−2))^2 + (0 − 9)^2 = (x + 2)^2 + (−9)^2 = (x + 2)^2 + 81.

Set PR^2 = QR^2:
(x − 2)^2 + 25 = (x + 2)^2 + 81.

Expand both sides:
(x^2 − 4x + 4) + 25 = (x^2 + 4x + 4) + 81
x^2 − 4x + 29 = x^2 + 4x + 85.

Subtract x^2 from both sides and collect like terms:
−4x + 29 = 4x + 85
29 − 85 = 8x
−56 = 8x
x = −7.

Final answer

The required point on the x-axis is (−7, 0).

Question  
Find the distances between the following points.
i. A(a, 0), B(0, a)  
ii. P(−6, −3), Q(−1, 9)  
iii. R(−3a, a), S(a, −2a)

Method  
Distance formula: For points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2),
d = sqrt[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2].
Note: when the result contains a factor a, the distance is |a| times the numeric factor (distance is always non‑negative).

Working

i. A(a, 0) and B(0, a)
- x2 − x1 = 0 − a = −a, y2 − y1 = a − 0 = a
- d(A, B) = sqrt[ (−a)^2 + (a)^2 ] = sqrt[ a^2 + a^2 ] = sqrt[ 2a^2 ] = |a|·sqrt(2).
(If a > 0 this equals a√2.)

ii. P(−6, −3) and Q(−1, 9)
- x2 − x1 = −1 − (−6) = 5, y2 − y1 = 9 − (−3) = 12
- d(P, Q) = sqrt[ 5^2 + 12^2 ] = sqrt[ 25 + 144 ] = sqrt[169] = 13.

iii. R(−3a, a) and S(a, −2a)
- x2 − x1 = a − (−3a) = 4a, y2 − y1 = −2a − a = −3a
- d(R, S) = sqrt[ (4a)^2 + (−3a)^2 ] = sqrt[ 16a^2 + 9a^2 ] = sqrt[ 25a^2 ] = 5|a|.

Final answer
i. d(A, B) = |a|·√2  
ii. d(P, Q) = 13 units  
iii. d(R, S) = 5|a|

Question  
Find the coordinates of the circumcentre of the triangle with vertices A(−3, 1), B(0, −2) and C(1, 3).

Method  
The circumcentre O(h, k) is equidistant from all three vertices. Set OA^2 = OB^2 and OB^2 = OC^2 (using squared distances to avoid square roots) and solve the resulting linear system for h and k.

Working
1. Use OA^2 = OB^2.

   (h + 3)^2 + (k − 1)^2 = h^2 + (k + 2)^2

   Expand both sides:
   h^2 + 6h + 9 + k^2 − 2k + 1 = h^2 + k^2 + 4k + 4

   Cancel h^2 and k^2, then simplify:
   6h + 10 − 2k = 4k + 4
   6h + 6 = 6k
   Divide by 6:
   h − k = −1   ...(1)

2. Use OB^2 = OC^2.

   h^2 + (k + 2)^2 = (h − 1)^2 + (k − 3)^2

   Expand:
   h^2 + k^2 + 4k + 4 = h^2 − 2h + 1 + k^2 − 6k + 9

   Cancel h^2 and k^2, then simplify:
   4k + 4 = −2h + 1 − 6k + 9
   2h + 10k = 6
   Divide by 2:
   h + 5k = 3   ...(2)

3. Solve the linear system (1) and (2).

   From (1): h = k − 1. Substitute into (2):
   (k − 1) + 5k = 3
   6k − 1 = 3
   6k = 4
   k = 4/6 = 2/3

   Then h = k − 1 = 2/3 − 1 = −1/3

Final answer  
The circumcentre is O(−1/3, 2/3).

Question
In the following examples, can the segment joining the given points form a triangle? If a triangle is formed, state its type (by side lengths).

i. L(6, 4), M(−5, −3), N(−6, 8)
ii. P(−2, −6), Q(−4, −2), R(−5, 0)
iii. A(2 − √, 2 − √), B(−2 − √, −2 − √), C(6 − √, 6 − √)

Method
- To check whether three points form a triangle, verify they are not collinear.
- Ways to test collinearity:
  - Compare slopes of two pairs of points: if slopes are equal, points are collinear (unless denominator zero handled).
  - Or compute pairwise distances and check if one distance equals the sum of the other two (then one point lies between the other two).
- If not collinear, compute the three side lengths. If all three are different → scalene; two equal → isosceles; all three equal → equilateral. Also check if Pythagorean relation holds for a right triangle.

Working

i. L(6,4), M(−5,−3), N(−6,8)

Compute pairwise distances using distance formula d((x1,y1),(x2,y2)) = √[(x1−x2)^2 + (y1−y2)^2].

- d(L,M) = √[(6 − (−5))^2 + (4 − (−3))^2]
         = √[(11)^2 + (7)^2] = √(121 + 49) = √170.

- d(M,N) = √[ (−5 − (−6))^2 + (−3 − 8)^2 ]
         = √[ (1)^2 + (−11)^2 ] = √(1 + 121) = √122.

- d(L,N) = √[ (6 − (−6))^2 + (4 − 8)^2 ]
         = √[ (12)^2 + (−4)^2 ] = √(144 + 16) = √160.

Check triangle inequality (any two sides sum greater than third):
- √122 + √160 > √170 (numerically about 11.05 + 12.65 > 13.04) — true.
- Similar checks hold for other combinations.

Thus the three points are not collinear and do form a triangle.

Compare side lengths:
√170 ≈ 13.038, √160 ≈ 12.649, √122 ≈ 11.045 — all three are different. So the triangle is scalene.

ii. P(−2,−6), Q(−4,−2), R(−5,0)

Find slopes to test collinearity.
- Slope PQ = (−2 − (−6)) / (−4 − (−2)) = 4 / (−2) = −2.
- Slope QR = (0 − (−2)) / (−5 − (−4)) = 2 / (−1) = −2.

Slopes PQ and QR are equal, so P, Q, R lie on the same straight line ⇒ they are collinear. Equivalently, check distances:
- d(P,Q) = √[(−2 − (−4))^2 + (−6 − (−2))^2] = √(2^2 + (−4)^2) = √20 = 2√5.
- d(Q,R) = √[(−4 − (−5))^2 + (−2 − 0)^2] = √(1^2 + (−2)^2) = √5.
- d(P,R) = √[(−2 − (−5))^2 + (−6 − 0)^2] = √(3^2 + (−6)^2) = √45 = 3√5.

Notice d(P,Q) + d(Q,R) = 2√5 + √5 = 3√5 = d(P,R), so Q lies between P and R. Therefore no triangle can be formed.

iii. A(2 − √, 2 − √), B(−2 − √, −2 − √), C(6 − √, 6 − √)

(Here the symbol "√" appears without a specified radicand. We do not need the radicand to test collinearity because the same symbol appears in every coordinate and cancels in differences.)

Observe all three points have coordinates of the form (k − r, k − r) with the same r. Thus each point lies on the line y = x (shifted by the same −r cancels), so they are all on the same straight line.

More directly using x-coordinates:
- x_B − x_A = (−2 − r) − (2 − r) = −4
- x_C − x_B = (6 − r) − (−2 − r) = 8

Since the changes in x and y are equal for each pair, slope AB = 1 and slope BC = 1. Thus A, B, C are collinear.

Also distances satisfy: |x_B − x_A| = 4, |x_C − x_A| = 4, |x_C − x_B| = 8, so d(AB) + d(AC) = d(BC). Therefore the three points lie on one line and do not form a triangle.

Final answer
i. Yes. Points L, M, N are non‑collinear and form a triangle. Since all three side lengths are different, ΔLMN is a scalene triangle.

ii. No. Points P, Q, R are collinear (Q lies between P and R); they do not form a triangle.

iii. No. Points A, B, C are collinear (all lie on the same line y = x after cancelling the common "√" term); they do not form a triangle.

Method

Use the slope formula for two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1).

Question  
Show that the line joining the points A(4, 8) and B(5, 5) is parallel to the line joining the points C(2, 4) and D(1, 7).

Method  
Two non-vertical lines in the plane are parallel exactly when they have equal slopes. Use the slope formula m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1) to find slopes of AB and CD and compare them.

Diagram cue  
The diagram only shows the segments AB and CD; no additional numerical information is needed beyond the given coordinates.

Working
1. Slope of AB:
   - Take A(4, 8) and B(5, 5).
   - m_AB = (y_B − y_A) / (x_B − x_A) = (5 − 8) / (5 − 4) = (−3) / 1 = −3.

2. Slope of CD:
   - Take C(2, 4) and D(1, 7).
   - m_CD = (y_D − y_C) / (x_D − x_C) = (7 − 4) / (1 − 2) = 3 / (−1) = −3.

3. Compare:
   - m_AB = −3 and m_CD = −3, so m_AB = m_CD.

Final answer  
Since the slopes of AB and CD are equal (both −3), the lines AB and CD are parallel. Hence AB ∥ CD.

Question  
Show that points P(1, −2), Q(5, 2), R(3, −1), S(−1, −5) are the vertices of a parallelogram.

Method  
Use coordinates to compute the vectors representing the sides. If the two opposite side vectors are equal (same components) then each pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, so the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

Working
1. Compute vector PQ = Q − P:
   PQ = (5 − 1, 2 − (−2)) = (4, 4).

2. Compute vector SR = R − S:
   SR = (3 − (−1), −1 − (−5)) = (4, 4).

   So PQ = SR (they have the same components), hence PQ and SR are equal and parallel.

3. Compute vector QR = R − Q:
   QR = (3 − 5, −1 − 2) = (−2, −3).

4. Compute vector PS = S − P:
   PS = (−1 − 1, −5 − (−2)) = (−2, −3).

   So QR = PS, hence QR and PS are equal and parallel.

Since both pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel, PQRS is a parallelogram.

Final answer  
Points P(1, −2), Q(5, 2), R(3, −1), S(−1, −5) are the vertices of a parallelogram.

Show that the quadrilateral PQRS with P(2, 1), Q(−1, 3), R(−5, −3) and S(−2, −5) is a rectangle.

Method  
1. Show PQRS is a parallelogram by checking that opposite sides are parallel (or equal as vectors).  
2. Show one pair of adjacent sides are perpendicular (product of their slopes = −1). A parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle.

Working
1. Compute vectors for the sides.
- Vector PQ = Q − P = (−1 − 2, 3 − 1) = (−3, 2).
- Vector QR = R − Q = (−5 − (−1), −3 − 3) = (−4, −6).
- Vector RS = S − R = (−2 − (−5), −5 − (−3)) = (3, −2).
- Vector SP = P − S = (2 − (−2), 1 − (−5)) = (4, 6) so PS = S − P = (−4, −6).

2. Check opposite sides are parallel (vectors are scalar multiples).
- RS = (3, −2) = −1·(−3, 2) = −PQ, so RS is parallel to PQ and |RS| = |PQ|.
- PS = (−4, −6) = QR, so PS is parallel to QR and |PS| = |QR|.

Hence both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so PQRS is a parallelogram.

3. Check perpendicularity of adjacent sides by slopes.
- Slope of PQ = (3 − 1)/(−1 − 2) = 2/(−3) = −2/3.
- Slope of QR = (−3 − 3)/(−5 − (−1)) = (−6)/(−4) = 3/2.
- Product of slopes = (−2/3)·(3/2) = −1, so PQ ⟂ QR.

Because PQRS is a parallelogram and one interior angle (at Q) is a right angle, all angles are right angles; therefore PQRS is a rectangle.

Final answer  
PQRS is a rectangle.

Question  
Find the lengths of the medians of a triangle with vertices A(−1, 1), B(5, −3) and C(3, 5).

Method  
A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Use the midpoint formula to find those midpoints and the distance formula to find the length of each median.  
- Midpoint of points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2).  
- Distance between (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is sqrt[(x2−x1)^2 + (y2−y1)^2].

Working
1. Find midpoints of the sides.
- Midpoint D of BC:
  D = ((5+3)/2, (−3+5)/2) = (4, 1).
- Midpoint E of AC:
  E = ((−1+3)/2, (1+5)/2) = (1, 3).
- Midpoint F of AB:
  F = ((−1+5)/2, (1+ (−3))/2) = (2, −1).

2. Compute lengths of medians AD, BE, CF.

- AD: distance between A(−1,1) and D(4,1)
  AD = sqrt[(4 − (−1))^2 + (1 − 1)^2] = sqrt[5^2 + 0^2] = 5.

- BE: distance between B(5,−3) and E(1,3)
  BE = sqrt[(1 − 5)^2 + (3 − (−3))^2] = sqrt[(−4)^2 + 6^2] = sqrt[16 + 36] = sqrt(52) = 2√13.

- CF: distance between C(3,5) and F(2,−1)
  CF = sqrt[(2 − 3)^2 + (−1 − 5)^2] = sqrt[(−1)^2 + (−6)^2] = sqrt[1 + 36] = √37.

Final answer  
Lengths of the medians are: AD = 5 units, BE = 2√13 units, CF = √37 units.

Question  
Find the coordinates of the centroid of a triangle whose midpoints of the sides are D(−7, 6), E(8, 5) and F(2, −2).

Method  
Let the vertices be A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), C(x3, y3). Use the midpoint formula for each given midpoint to get linear equations in x1, x2, x3 and y1, y2, y3. Sum the three equations for x and for y to find x1 + x2 + x3 and y1 + y2 + y3. The centroid G has coordinates ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3).

Working
- D is the midpoint of BC, so
  (x2 + x3)/2 = −7  ⇒ x2 + x3 = −14
  (y2 + y3)/2 = 6   ⇒ y2 + y3 = 12

- E is the midpoint of AC, so
  (x1 + x3)/2 = 8   ⇒ x1 + x3 = 16
  (y1 + y3)/2 = 5   ⇒ y1 + y3 = 10

- F is the midpoint of AB, so
  (x1 + x2)/2 = 2   ⇒ x1 + x2 = 4
  (y1 + y2)/2 = −2  ⇒ y1 + y2 = −4

Add the three x-equations:
(x2 + x3) + (x1 + x3) + (x1 + x2) = −14 + 16 + 4
2(x1 + x2 + x3) = 6  ⇒  x1 + x2 + x3 = 3

Add the three y-equations:
(y2 + y3) + (y1 + y3) + (y1 + y2) = 12 + 10 + (−4)
2(y1 + y2 + y3) = 18  ⇒  y1 + y2 + y3 = 9

Centroid G = ( (x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3 ) = (3/3, 9/3) = (1, 3).

Final answer  
The coordinates of the centroid are (1, 3).

Question 15

Given:
A(4, −1), B(6, 0), C(7, −2), D(5, −3).

To prove:
Points A, B, C, D are vertices of a square.

Proof / Steps:

1. Compute the lengths of the four sides using distance formula.
   - AB = √[(6 − 4)² + (0 − (−1))²] = √[2² + 1²] = √(4 + 1) = √5.
   - BC = √[(7 − 6)² + (−2 − 0)²] = √[1² + (−2)²] = √(1 + 4) = √5.
   - CD = √[(5 − 7)² + (−3 − (−2))²] = √[(−2)² + (−1)²] = √(4 + 1) = √5.
   - DA = √[(4 − 5)² + (−1 − (−3))²] = √[(−1)² + 2²] = √(1 + 4) = √5.

   Thus AB = BC = CD = DA = √5. All four sides are equal.

2. Show one pair of adjacent sides is perpendicular (so all angles are right in a rhombus with equal sides).
   - Slope of AB = (0 − (−1)) / (6 − 4) = 1 / 2.
   - Slope of BC = (−2 − 0) / (7 − 6) = −2 / 1 = −2.
   - Product of slopes = (1/2) × (−2) = −1, so AB ⟂ BC.

   Since two adjacent sides are equal in length and are perpendicular, the quadrilateral is a square.

(As an additional check: diagonals AC and BD have equal lengths.)
   - AC = √[(7 − 4)² + (−2 − (−1))²] = √[3² + (−1)²] = √10.
   - BD = √[(5 − 6)² + (−3 − 0)²] = √[(−1)² + (−3)²] = √10.
   The diagonals are equal (and their slopes are negative reciprocals, so they are perpendicular), consistent with a square.

Result:
□ABCD is a square.

Question
Find the coordinates of the circumcentre and the radius of the circumcircle of triangle ABC where A(7, 1), B(3, 5) and C(2, 0).

Method
The circumcentre is the intersection point of the perpendicular bisectors of any two sides of the triangle. 
1. Find the perpendicular bisector of AB.
2. Find the perpendicular bisector of BC.
3. Solve their equations to get the circumcentre O(h, k).
4. Compute the distance from O to any vertex (say A) to get the circumradius.

Working
1. Side AB
- Midpoint of AB: M_AB = ((7+3)/2, (1+5)/2) = (5, 3).
- Slope of AB: (5 − 1)/(3 − 7) = 4/(-4) = −1. 
- Perpendicular bisector of AB has slope 1 (negative reciprocal of −1) and passes through (5,3).
  Equation: y − 3 = 1·(x − 5) ⇒ y = x − 2.   (1)

2. Side BC
- Midpoint of BC: M_BC = ((3+2)/2, (5+0)/2) = (5/2, 5/2).
- Slope of BC: (0 − 5)/(2 − 3) = −5/−1 = 5.
- Perpendicular bisector of BC has slope −1/5 and passes through (5/2, 5/2).
  Equation: y − 5/2 = (−1/5)(x − 5/2).
  Simplify right side: y = 5/2 − (1/5)(x − 5/2) = 5/2 − x/5 + 1/2 = 3 − x/5.   (2)

3. Intersection of (1) and (2)
Set x − 2 = 3 − x/5.
Bring terms together: x + x/5 = 5 ⇒ (6/5)x = 5 ⇒ x = 5·(5/6) = 25/6.
Then y = x − 2 = 25/6 − 12/6 = 13/6.

Thus circumcentre O = (25/6, 13/6).

4. Circumradius
Distance OA:
Vector OA = A − O = (7 − 25/6, 1 − 13/6) = (17/6, −7/6).
Radius = sqrt[(17/6)^2 + (−7/6)^2] = (1/6) sqrt(17^2 + 7^2) = (1/6) sqrt(289 + 49) = (1/6) sqrt(338).
Since 338 = 2·169 = 2·13^2, sqrt(338) = 13√2. Therefore radius = 13√2 / 6.

Final answer
- Circumcentre O = (25/6, 13/6).
- Circumradius r = 13√2 / 6 units.

Question
Given A(4, −3), B(8, 5). Find the coordinates of the point C that divides segment AB in the ratio 3 : 1 (internally).

Method
Let C be the point on AB such that AC : CB = 3 : 1. If a point divides the segment from A to B in the ratio m : n (internally), its position measured from A is a fraction m/(m+n) of the way from A to B. So
C = A + [m/(m+n)](B − A).

(If a diagram is provided, Diagram cue: we only use the given coordinates A and B and the ratio 3:1 to compute C; no other diagram measurements are needed.)

Working
A = (4, −3), B = (8, 5). Here m = 3, n = 1, so the fraction from A toward B is 3/(3+1) = 3/4.

Vector B − A = (8 − 4, 5 − (−3)) = (4, 8).
Multiply by 3/4: (3/4)·(4, 8) = (3, 6).

Now add to A:
C = A + (3, 6) = (4 + 3, −3 + 6) = (7, 3).

Final answer
The point that divides AB in the ratio 3 : 1 is C(7, 3).
